list_servers.title: List PostgreSQL flexible servers in the subscription
list_servers.description: Every Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server in the subscription, with its major version, SKU, storage, state and `fullyQualifiedDomainName` -- the host a client connects to. A `state` of `Stopped` explains a server that is not answering without anything being broken.

output.description: Every PostgreSQL flexible server in the subscription.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties (version, state, fullyQualifiedDomainName, storage, backup, highAvailability, network).

list_servers_in_group.title: List PostgreSQL servers in a resource group
list_servers_in_group.description: The PostgreSQL flexible servers in one resource group, with the same detail as list_servers. Cheaper than scanning the subscription when the group is known.

resource_group.description: The resource group to look in.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties.

get_server.title: Get a PostgreSQL flexible server
get_server.description:
One server in full: PostgreSQL major version, compute SKU, storage size and auto-grow setting, backup retention and geo-redundancy, high availability mode, network configuration and administrator login.
`storage.autoGrow` is worth reading early: without it, a server whose disk fills stops accepting writes, and PostgreSQL's error does not point at Azure.

server_name.description: The server name, without the .postgres.database.azure.com suffix.

sku.description: name and tier -- Burstable, GeneralPurpose or MemoryOptimized.

properties.description: version, state, fullyQualifiedDomainName, administratorLogin, storage, backup, highAvailability, network and replicationRole.

create_or_update_server.title: Create a PostgreSQL flexible server
create_or_update_server.description:
Create a managed PostgreSQL server, or replace an existing one's configuration. The name becomes part of a public DNS name and is therefore globally unique -- test it with check_name_availability first.
`administrator_login_password` is settable here and at update_server and is never readable back; store it before making the call. Provisioning takes several minutes: poll get_server until `state` is `Ready`.
Storage can be grown later but never shrunk. Major version upgrades are a separate operation, so pick the version deliberately.
create_or_update_server.notes: The server name must be globally unique. The admin password can never be read back.

resource_group.description: The resource group to create the server in.

server_name.description: The server name -- globally unique, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.

administrator_login.description: The PostgreSQL administrator username. Cannot be changed later.

administrator_login_password.description: The administrator password. Never readable afterwards.

sku_name.description: Compute size, e.g. Standard_B1ms or Standard_D2ds_v5.

sku_tier.description: Compute tier. Burstable is cheapest and throttles under sustained load.

storage_size_gb.description: Storage in GB. Can be grown later, never shrunk.

storage_auto_grow.description: Grow storage automatically as it fills. Without it, a full disk stops writes.

backup_retention_days.description: Days of automatic backup to keep, 7 to 35.

geo_redundant_backup.description: Replicate backups to the paired region. Fixed at creation.

high_availability_mode.description: ZoneRedundant or SameZone standby. Roughly doubles the compute cost.

output.description: The server as created; provisioning continues asynchronously.

properties.description: state -- Creating at this point -- and fullyQualifiedDomainName once ready.

update_server.title: Scale or reconfigure a PostgreSQL server
update_server.description:
Merge a change into an existing server: a different compute SKU, more storage, new backup retention, a rotated administrator password, or high availability on or off.
A compute SKU change restarts the server -- a brief outage. Storage can only grow. Turning high availability on provisions a standby and roughly doubles the compute bill.
update_server.notes: A SKU change restarts the server. Storage cannot be reduced.

sku_name.description: New compute size. Changing it restarts the server.

storage_size_gb.description: New storage size in GB. Must be larger than the current one.

storage_auto_grow.description: Turn storage auto-grow on or off.

backup_retention_days.description: New backup retention in days, 7 to 35.

administrator_login_password.description: Rotate the administrator password. Breaks anything using the old one.

high_availability_mode.description: Turn high availability on or off.

properties.description: state -- Updating while the change lands.

delete_server.title: Delete a PostgreSQL server
delete_server.description: Destroy a PostgreSQL flexible server, every database on it, and its automatic backups. Irreversible -- there is no restorable-dropped list to recover from. If the data might still be wanted, run restore_server_to_point_in_time to a second server first, then delete this one.
delete_server.notes: Deletes the server's backups as well. There is no recovery afterwards.

start_server.title: Start a stopped PostgreSQL server
start_server.description: Bring a stopped server back online and resume compute billing. Asynchronous -- poll get_server until `state` is `Ready`. A server left stopped for 7 days is started by Azure automatically.

stop_server.title: Stop a PostgreSQL server
stop_server.description: Stop the server, halting compute billing; storage and backups keep billing. Every connection is dropped and nothing can connect until start_server. Azure restarts a stopped server automatically after 7 days, so this saves money overnight rather than mothballing a server.
stop_server.notes: Drops all connections. Azure auto-starts the server after 7 days.

restart_server.title: Restart a PostgreSQL server
restart_server.description:
Restart the server, which is what applies a static parameter change from update_configuration -- including `shared_preload_libraries`, the one several extensions need. Every connection is dropped and the server is unavailable for a minute or two.
On a high-availability server, restart_with_failover restarts by failing over to the standby, which is faster and doubles as a test that the standby works.
restart_server.notes: Drops all connections. The server is unavailable while it restarts.

restart_with_failover.description: Restart by failing over to the standby. Only valid on a high-availability server.

failover_mode.description: How to fail over when restart_with_failover is set.

list_databases.title: List the databases on a PostgreSQL server
list_databases.description: Every database on the server, with its encoding and collation. The built-in `postgres`, `azure_maintenance` and `azure_sys` databases appear here and are not yours to modify.

create_database.title: Create an empty database on a PostgreSQL server
create_database.description: Create a database on the server. It comes up empty -- schemas, tables, roles, grants and extensions all need a PostgreSQL client, which this connector is not. `UTF8` with `en_US.utf8` is the usual pairing.

server_name.description: The server to create the database on.

collation.description: Collation, which decides sorting and comparison. Fixed at creation.

delete_database.title: Drop a database from a PostgreSQL server
delete_database.description: Drop a database and everything in it. Irreversible short of restoring the whole server to a new one -- PostgreSQL flexible server has no per-database restore. Open connections to the database will make the drop fail.

database_name.description: The database to drop, with everything in it.

list_firewall_rules.title: List a PostgreSQL server's firewall rules
list_firewall_rules.description:
The IP ranges allowed to reach the server. Check this first when a client hangs or times out rather than being told its password is wrong. A rule with both addresses 0.0.0.0 is the "allow other Azure services" special case; 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 opens the server to the internet.
A server deployed into a virtual network has no firewall rules at all.

create_firewall_rule.title: Allow an IP range to reach a PostgreSQL server
create_firewall_rule.description:
Open the server to a range of client addresses. Keep it narrow -- 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 exposes the server to every address on the internet, with only the PostgreSQL password in the way.
This grants network reach only; the client still authenticates normally. Reusing a rule name replaces that rule.
create_firewall_rule.notes: Widening the range widens the attack surface. It grants no database privileges.

rule_name.description: A name for the rule. Reusing one replaces it.

start_ip_address.description: First address in the allowed range.

end_ip_address.description: Last address in the range; the same as the start for a single address.

delete_firewall_rule.title: Remove a PostgreSQL firewall rule
delete_firewall_rule.description: Close a previously allowed range. Clients in it lose access on their next connection attempt; existing connections are not cut. Check list_firewall_rules first to see which clients the rule was carrying.

list_configurations.title: List a PostgreSQL server's parameters
list_configurations.description:
Every server parameter with its current value, default, allowed values and the two flags that decide how to change it: `isDynamicConfig` (true means no restart needed) and `isReadOnly` (true means Azure will not let you change it).
This is where `azure.extensions` lives -- the allow-list that decides which extensions `CREATE EXTENSION` will accept -- along with `shared_preload_libraries`, `max_connections`, `log_min_duration_statement` and the rest of `postgresql.conf`.

output.description: Every server parameter and its metadata.

items.description: name and properties (value, defaultValue, allowedValues, dataType, source, isDynamicConfig, isReadOnly, unit).

get_configuration.title: Get one PostgreSQL server parameter
get_configuration.description: A single parameter's current value, default, allowed values and whether changing it needs a restart. Reading `azure.extensions` this way is the quickest check of why `CREATE EXTENSION` is being refused.

properties.description: value, defaultValue, allowedValues, source, isDynamicConfig and isReadOnly.

update_configuration.title: Change a PostgreSQL server parameter
update_configuration.description:
Set one server parameter. The two changes worth knowing about:
Setting `azure.extensions` to a comma-separated list -- `vector,postgis, pg_stat_statements` -- is what allows those extensions to be installed with `CREATE EXTENSION` afterwards. This is the fix for "extension is not allow-listed". It is a dynamic parameter, so it takes effect at once.
Setting `shared_preload_libraries` is static: it needs restart_server, and several extensions (pg_stat_statements, pg_cron) need to be in it as well as in azure.extensions.
Check `isDynamicConfig` on any other parameter before assuming the change has landed. Values outside `allowedValues` are rejected.
update_configuration.notes: A non-dynamic parameter only takes effect after restart_server, which drops all connections.

value.description: The new value. For azure.extensions this is a comma-separated extension list. Must be within the parameter's allowedValues.

source.description: user-override applies your value; system-default reverts to Azure's.

properties.description: value, source and isDynamicConfig -- check the last to know whether a restart is needed.

list_backups.title: List a PostgreSQL server's backups
list_backups.description: The automatic backups Azure holds for the server, each with its completion time and type. These are what restore_server_to_point_in_time draws on; the window is `backup.backupRetentionDays` from get_server and anything older is gone.

items.description: id, name and properties (backupType, completedTime, source).

restore_server_to_point_in_time.title: Restore a PostgreSQL server to a point in time
restore_server_to_point_in_time.description:
Create a NEW server from an existing one's backups as it stood at a given instant. Nothing is overwritten -- the source keeps running -- which makes this safe to reach for mid-incident, and it is the only recovery path PostgreSQL flexible server offers.
`restore_point_in_time` must be inside the source's retention window. The restore takes a while; poll get_server on the new name until `state` is `Ready`. The restored server carries the source's parameters and firewall rules.
restore_server_to_point_in_time.notes: Creates a second server, which bills separately from the source.

resource_group.description: The resource group to create the restored server in.

target_server_name.description: A name for the restored server. Globally unique, and must not already exist.

location.description: The region for the restored server.

source_server_id.description: ARM id of the server to restore from, from get_server.

restore_point_in_time.description: The instant to restore to, ISO 8601 UTC, inside the retention window.

properties.description: state -- Creating while the restore runs.

list_replicas.title: List a PostgreSQL server's read replicas
list_replicas.description: The read replicas of a server, each with its region, SKU and state. Replicas serve read traffic and lag behind the primary; `replicationRole` says whether a server is Primary or a replica. Promotion is a separate operation -- deleting the primary does not promote anything.

items.description: id, name, location, sku and properties (replicationRole, sourceServerResourceId, state).

list_entra_administrators.title: List a PostgreSQL server's Microsoft Entra administrators
list_entra_administrators.description: The Entra ID principals configured as administrators on the server -- users, groups or service principals that can authenticate with a token instead of a password. Worth reading before rotating the SQL admin password: if an Entra admin exists, there is a way in that does not depend on it.

items.description: name and properties (principalType, principalName, objectId, tenantId).

check_name_availability.title: Check whether a PostgreSQL server name is free
check_name_availability.description: PostgreSQL flexible server names become public DNS names and share one global namespace, so a name that looks obviously yours may be taken. This asks before a create fails on it, and the `reason` separates an invalid name from a taken one.

output.description: Whether the name is available, and why not if it is not.

nameAvailable.description: True when the name can be used.
